E1843.summary: In the Appendix, Atwood names the Universal Center as consciousness's own true Source and the source of all things.
E1843.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood speaks of consciousness drawn centrally coming to know “its own true Source, which is the Universal Center and source of all things” [APP ¶6]. So the Universal Center is identified with that true Source.

E1844.summary: What the adepts found to be in the fire of man's life; the text does not define it further.
E1844.body: Atwood reports that the adepts found “the Universal Efficient was in this fire” [IV.4 ¶4], the fire being man's life. She presents this with approval. The passage does not define the term further.

E1845.summary: What the Alchemists set out to rectify: an invisible vapor they compressed into a tangible Form, as distinct from the common elements of chemistry.
E1845.body: Atwood says the Alchemists aimed “to rectify the Universal Element, and compress its invisible vapor into a tangible Form” [IV.1 ¶47]. She sets this against the common elements of chemistry. In her account, then, the Universal Element starts as invisible and vaporous and the art gives it bodily form.

E1846.summary: In Khunrath's account, that with which the Azoth reanimates bodies that have been reduced to First Matter.
E1846.body: Quoting Khunrath, the text says the Azoth takes bodies reduced to First Matter and “reanimates them with the Universal Form” [IV.3 ¶28]. The Universal Form is therefore what gives those dissolved bodies new life.

E1847.summary: What appears in the mind during the work; the impress seen in the vessel serves as a secondary witness that confirms it.
E1847.body: In a footnote Atwood speaks of “this appearance of the Universal Idea in the mind” [III.3 n27], comparing it with the pattern seen in the Subject Waters. She treats the impress seen in the vessel as a secondary witness that confirms it. On this account the main evidence is in the mind, and what shows in the vessel only corroborates it.

E1848.summary: The one identity in which all things are identical, so every assertion of it is true; body, soul and spirit are born in it.
E1848.body: Atwood writes: “All is identical --- need we repeat it? --- in the Universal Identity, and every possible assertion of it will be true” [III.3 ¶67]. She also says body, soul and spirit are born in this identity. Readers listed “Unknown Identity” and “Identity” as variants, but the packet does not show them as forms of this headword.

E1849.summary: What the physiologists and alchemists are said to have proved by experiment, on ontological ground.
E1849.body: Atwood reports that the physiologists and alchemists “were said to prove the Universal Identity of Nature on the ontological ground” [II.4 ¶16]. In other words, they are said to have proved it experimentally. She gives this as a report (“were said”).

E1850.summary: The law under which fulfilment comes once the outer and inner worlds agree.
E1850.body: Atwood says that once the outer and inner worlds agree, the result is “a fulfillment under the Universal Law” [III.3 ¶82].

forms: Universal Law of Light in Nature
E1851.summary: The law that, according to Atwood, the philosophers' Stone shows at every stage: its origin, its development and its artificial preparation.
E1851.body: Atwood writes that “their Stone exhibits, alike in its origin, development and artificial preparation throughout, the Universal Law of Light in Nature” [IV.3 ¶27]. On this account the making of the Stone follows the same law of light that runs through nature.

E1852.summary: In the Appendix, matter that can be obtained at the focus of any of the three microcosmic centers.
E1852.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “The universal matter is obtainable at the focus of either center.” [APP ¶95]. The centers meant are the three microcosmic centers.

E1853.summary: A medicine, described by several cited authorities, that preserves health and cures all diseases, and that comes from the true Mercury of the philosophers.
E1853.body:
Three cited authorities speak of it. None of these passages is in Atwood's own voice.

- **The Scholiast:** “the universal medicine is concreted” from things full of the balsam of nature. It preserves health and roots out diseases [I.3 n61].
- **Eudoxus:** the true Mercury of the philosophers is what “will give you the fixed Sulphur and the Universal Medicine” [IV.3 ¶16]. The same passage also speaks of “the medicine of the Third order” and “the three medicines”.
- **Eirenaeus:** the accomplished artist would have “a universal medicine, moreover, capable of curing all diseases” [IV.3 ¶26].

E1854.summary: The medium at work in mesmerism. Mesmerists use it as it naturally comes, while the ancients dissolved it further.
E1854.body: Atwood treats the Universal Medium as what operates in mesmerism. It can be improved, can rise or sink, and has a right determination. She notes that the mesmerists take it as they find it: “as respects the Universal Medium, they even, who believe in such a thing, take it as it presents itself naturally” [II.2 ¶7]. The ancients, by contrast, worked “to dissolve the medium more entirely” [II.2 ¶8]. The contrast suggests that she sees further dissolution of this medium as part of the ancient method that modern mesmerism lacks.

E1855.summary: The life-giving substance that all beings live in without knowing it. It is hidden in natural generation and is to be known from within.
E1855.body: Atwood speaks of those who seek “to know intrinsical within themselves the substance of that Universal Nature in which they, with all beings in common, as it were, unconsciously live” [I.3 n8]. She says this nature is hidden in natural generation and must be known from within. She also applies Apuleius' praise of Isis to it: “All which is readily admissible of the Universal Nature” [II.4 ¶19]. Here Universal Nature is the life-supplying source that we are drawn out of and that keeps us in being, and it is revealed in the Epopteia.

E1856.summary: What Nature carries sealed in her own vessel through dissolution to resurrection. It is the third of three hypostatic relations, “the All in all”.
E1856.body: Atwood speaks of Nature's vessel, “in which she bears her Universal Offspring, hermetically sealed” [III.3 ¶65], from dissolution through to resurrection. She also names it as the third hypostatic relation alongside agent and patient: “that universal offspring which is the All in all, without foreign admixture” [III.3 ¶67].

E1857.summary: The reason that man holds within himself. The ancients magnified it, and it answers the sceptical individual intellect when that intellect is humble.
E1857.body: Quoting Agrippa, the text says man “contains the Universal Reason within himself” [II.1 ¶9], and that this makes him God's image. In her own voice, Atwood refers to “the Universal Reason so magnified and its ethereal vehicle” [II.1 ¶32] by the ancients, and admits it offers the senses very little evidence. In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer) she writes: “The Universal Reason condescends to answer it when not self-seeking and too proud to know.” [APP ¶116]. The “it” is the individual, sceptical intellect.

E1858.summary: The science Lully is said to have come to late in life. It is also the state, together with integrity, to which the central work restores the mind.
E1858.body: Atwood writes: “Raymond Lully is supposed to have become acquainted with Arnold, and the Universal Science, late in life” [I.1 ¶46]. The context is Lully's turn to alchemy, but the text does not say outright that the Universal Science is alchemy. Elsewhere she says the central work “restores the human mind to integrity and universal science” [IV.4 ¶17].

E1859.summary: The soul hidden within Nature, which can be called her temple. The Ether is its vestibule or vehicle.
E1859.body: Atwood speaks of “the universal soul of the world, which is occultly suspended in Nature, and may be called her temple” [III.1 ¶5]. So it is identified with Nature's temple [III.1 ¶5]. She describes the Ether as its vestibule or vehicle.

E1860.summary: What man, through the virtue within him, could prove and magnify. According to Atwood, doing so was the foundation of the magistery.
E1860.body: Atwood says man “nor yet surmises the virtue that is in him, to prove and magnify the Universal Source” [II.1 ¶8]. She presents proving and magnifying this Source as the foundation of the magistery.

E1861.summary: The common source of the First Matter, metals and all things. It is a passive middle substance present everywhere in nature, which art can collect, rectify and perfect.
E1861.body:
Atwood speaks of the Universal Spirit throughout the book.

**Source and identities**
- The First Matter is generated by “active and passive relations of the Universal Spirit” [I.2 ¶31]. In its common state the Spirit is, “as the Spirit is in nature, said to be everywhere” [I.2 ¶40].
- It is the common source of metals and of all things: “from metalline seeds out of the Universal Spirit or Mercury” [I.2 ¶49]. This identifies it with Mercury.
- She adds that “without this spirit growth is impossible, or transmutation or increase” [I.2 ¶49].

**Nature**
- “the properties of the Universal Spirit are abstrusely included in all existence” [I.3 n4]. They can be understood only through the Spirit's own inner analysis and “introverted light”. The “central experience” within it cannot be found without God [I.3 n4].
- “this Universal Spirit is described as a middle substance --- passive, undetermined, susceptible of conversion and all extremes” [II.2 ¶26]. That is why art can perfect it.

**In the work**
- She speaks of “the Universal Spirit, which has been so often fermented, rectified, and recalcined” [IV.3 ¶29], until its central force acts at the circumference. The passage leaves open whether the Spirit is the common origin of the vivific Ens and of what the Ens assimilates, or is the Ens itself.

**Appendix** (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer)
- “The Universal Spirit is in one form the Principle of all growth” [APP ¶4]. It can be collected and brought to bear on a germ.
- The Hermetic Philosophy experiments into this Spirit through man, because “you must have the Universal developed in you before you can understand the Universal” [APP ¶65].

E1862.summary: The spirit by which light can be multiplied; knowledge of it applied in the mineral kingdom produced gold. It is the subject of Vaughan's Anima Magia Abscondita.
E1862.body: Atwood refers to the “miraculous multiplicability of light by the universal spirit of nature” [I.1 ¶38]. She says that knowledge of this spirit, applied in the mineral kingdom, produced gold. She also names it as the subject of Vaughan's Anima Magia Abscondita: “the universal spirit of nature, with its strange, abstruse, and miraculous ascent and descent” [I.1 ¶74]. The text does not explain this ascent and descent.

E1863.summary: The one subject of the Hermetic art and the foundation of its experiment, identified with the first matter. It exists in nature, can be nourished in Man, and its concentrated virtue is the Stone.
E1863.body:
According to the alchemists, the contradictory epitaphs describe “the properties of their universal subject” [I.1 ¶24]. Atwood puts off explaining this until later.

In her own voice:
- She identifies it with the first matter: “their Universal Subject or first matter” [I.2 ¶7].
- “this Universal Subject is the alleged foundation of the whole Hermetic experiment” [I.2 ¶8]. It is both what is transmuted and, once freed into its proper essentiality, what transmutes.
- Some pseudo-alchemists caught “glimpses of the Universal Subject” [II.1 ¶6] and still failed.
- The art's analysis is “the whole metaphysico-chemical analysis of the Universal Subject” [III.2 ¶20].
- It is the one subject underlying all Species, and transmutation concerns it: “there is a Universal Subject in nature, and that Subject is susceptible of nourishment in Man” [IV.4 ¶10]. Its concentrated virtue is the Stone.

E1864.summary: In the Appendix, the power the mind becomes related to when it enters the third life, so that it can act out that power's will.
E1864.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says that the mind entering the third life becomes “related to the Universal Vitalizing Power, and so can act Its will” [APP ¶3].

E1865.summary: In the Appendix, the agent of the Work, at war with the self-will. It dissolves the false forms and reproduces the faculties transmuted. It is identified with the great Salt Sea and Wisdom.
E1865.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood writes: “The Universal Will being represented as agent dissolves the false forms in the self-will represented as patient.” [APP ¶94]. It destroys the faculties and false forms and then reproduces them transmuted. She identifies it as “The great Salt Sea (Wisdom, the Universal Will)” [APP ¶94]. In plain terms, the agent–patient language of the Work is here read as the universal will acting on the individual self-will.

E1866.summary: General truths present in the mind independently of the senses. Atwood offers them as evidence of a higher reality and as grounds for her inquiry.
E1866.body: Atwood says “this subsistence of Universals in the human mind deserves to be profoundly considered” [II.1 ¶34]. She cites “the independent evidence of Universals in the human intellect” [II.1 ¶39] as proof of a higher kind of evidence and of a latent superstantial nature. On her account, the fact that the soul perceives universals shows it can act without phantasy, and “they reveal in us a necessity of Being beyond present experience” [II.2 ¶13]. This helps her introduce the Idea of Wisdom. Later she gives “the natural subsistence of Universals in the human mind” [IV.4 ¶14] as a ground of probability for the inquiry.

E1867.summary: In the Zohar's account, the divine hypostasis before it is manifested: hidden in the Infinite, unknown while the point of Light remains subjective. It has several names, including the Ancient of Days.
E1867.body: The text cites the Zohar here; this is not Atwood's own voice. The divine is described as hidden in the Infinite, without mind, figure or Being, and: “whilst the point of Light remains within subjective and inseparate, he is unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. Even when seen, “under this form by which he is seen, he remains still unknown” [III.2 ¶3]. The same passage gives his names: “in this sense he is called the Ancient of Days, the White Head, the Old Man by excellence, the Mystery of Mysteries” [III.2 ¶3].

E1868.summary: An unnamed voice, cited with “Alchemy has been declared”, that supports Atwood's view of Alchemy as the way to enter and discover Truth.
E1868.body: Atwood cites an unnamed declaration calling Alchemy “the only true glass of the mind” [IV.4 ¶12]. She uses it to support her view that Alchemy is the way to enter and discover Truth.

E1869.summary: An unnamed source, cited with “as it is narrated”, that supports the claim that by the Divine Will man has the mind and manual skill to bring about all things.
E1869.body: Atwood cites an unnamed narration (“as it is narrated”) to support the claim that, by the Divine Will, man has mind and manual efficacy to effect all things [IV.4 ¶3].

E1870.summary: An unnamed speaker, introduced with “he ... who said”, whose saying supports the idea that the search for Wisdom starts by setting the mind in motion.
E1870.body: Atwood quotes an unnamed speaker: “the first step of philosophy is to set the mind a-going” [III.1 ¶8]. She uses it to support the idea that the search for Wisdom starts by setting the mind in motion.

E1871.summary: In the Appendix, the region where the Ideas are, which the spirit in the medial life sees as its azure sky.
E1871.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood places the Ideas in “the Upper Ether, where the Ideas are” [APP ¶15]. To the spirit in the medial life it appears as its azure sky.

forms: Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret
E1872.summary: Urbigeranus, author of the Hermetic Secret, cited for calling the labor a labor of Hercules that cannot be done without the Theory of the Arcanum.
E1872.body:
Atwood cites Urbigeranus, the author of the Hermetic Secret, for two points [IV.1 ¶7]:
- He calls the labor a labor of Hercules.
- Along with “these Adepts”, he holds that it is impossible without the Theory of their Arcanum.

She uses him to support how difficult the work is and that it depends on theory.
